National Laboratory of the Rockies | 15 Propane Vehicle Considerations Propane Vehicle Considerations • Propane has a high-octane rating and can support spark-ignited internal combustion engines • Vehicle Options ◦ A variety of medium- and heavy-duty propane vehicle models are available. ◦ Gasoline vehicles can economically, reliably, and safely be converted for propane operation using qualified system retrofitters. ◦ Driving range is comparable to conventionally fueled vehicles. • Propane vehicles can cost more than comparable gasoline vehicles, but the cost of the fuel is typically lower than that of gasoline, so the return on Illustration by Josh Bauer, NREL investment can be short. • Additional information on propane vehicles Source: Alternative Fuels Data Center, Propane Vehicles, n.d. National Laboratory of the Rockies | 16 Propane Vehicle Fueling Propane Vehicle Fueling • The U.S. Department of Energy’s Alternative Fuels Data Center (AFDC) Station Locator tool provides information on public and private propane fueling stations. • Fleets may use existing public infrastructure or establish private infrastructure and pricing structures with local propane marketers. • At primary fueling sites, propane prices per gallon are often lower than gasoline prices. Buses fueling at a propane station in Colorado. • Propane used for transportation is associated with reduced Photo: Ryan Texer, Adams County School District levels of certain pollutants compared to conventional fuels. • Propane can provide safety and public health benefits; spilled fuel presents no threat to surface water, groundwater or soil. Source: Alternative Fuels Data Center, Propane Fueling Stations, n.d. Photo: Werner Slocum, NREL • Reduced noise. Source: Alternative Fuels Data Center, Propane School Bus Deployment in Pennsylvania Showcases Environmental and Economic Benefits, 2023 National Laboratory of the Rockies | 18 Fuel Cell Electric Vehicles Fuel Cell Electric Vehicles • Fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs) use hydrogen, which can be produced from a variety of energy sources and is used in fuel cells to generate electricity. • FCEVs have higher energy conversion efficiency than conventional internal combustion engine vehicles. • Light-duty FCEVs can be refueled at retail stations in under 5 minutes and typically provide a driving range exceeding 300 miles. • Medium- and heavy-duty FCEVs can accommodate bigger tanks, however, they may face weight limitations due U.S. Department of Transportation regulations that could reduce the total load potential. • Light-duty FCEVs are commercially available in limited quantities. Photo by Dennis Schroeder, NREL • The FCEV market is emerging for buses, marine vessels, ground support equipment, medium- and heavy-duty trucks, material handling equipment
